title: World Religions & Belief Systems
description: Explore the world's major religious traditions with respect, curiosity, and an open mind. All religions are treated with equal dignity.
disclaimer: This content is presented for educational purposes. All faiths are described respectfully and without bias.

islam.name: Islam
islam.summary: Islam is a monotheistic faith founded on the teachings revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The Arabic word 'Islam' means 'submission' or 'peace through submission to God'. Muslims believe in one God (Allah in Arabic) and that Muhammad ﷺ was His final prophet.

history.event: Birth of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in Mecca
First revelation of the Quran; beginning of Islamic prophethood
Hijra — migration from Mecca to Medina; start of the Islamic calendar
Peaceful conquest of Mecca; spread of Islam across the Arabian Peninsula
Death of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; Abu Bakr becomes first Caliph
Rapid spread of Islam across the Middle East, North Africa, Persia, and Spain
Abbasid Caliphate — Golden Age of Islamic science, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy
Ottoman Empire captures Constantinople; Ottoman Caliphate established
Dissolution of the Ottoman Caliphate; modern nation-states form across the Muslim world

six_pillars_of_faith: Belief in revealed scriptures (Quran, and earlier scriptures)
Belief in prophets (from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ)
Belief in the Day of Judgement
five_pillars: Hajj — pilgrimage to Mecca (once in a lifetime if able)

festivals.name: Eid ul-Fitr
festivals.description: Festival celebrating the end of the month-long fast of Ramadan. Families gather, special prayers are offered, gifts are exchanged, and food is shared.

festivals.name: Eid ul-Adha
festivals.description: Festival of Sacrifice commemorating Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son. Families sacrifice an animal and distribute the meat to family, neighbours, and the poor.

festivals.name: Laylat ul-Qadr
festivals.description: Night of Power — believed to be when the first verses of the Quran were revealed. Considered better than a thousand months; Muslims spend the night in prayer and reflection.

festivals.name: Mawlid un-Nabi
festivals.description: Celebration of the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ birthday, observed in many parts of the Muslim world with gatherings, poems, and praise.

sacred_texts.name: The Quran
sacred_texts.description: The central holy book of Islam — the direct word of God revealed to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through the Angel Jibreel over 23 years. Memorised in its entirety by millions (Hafiz). Written in classical Arabic.

sacred_texts.name: Hadith
sacred_texts.description: Collections of sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, recorded by companions. Major collections include Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

sacred_texts.name: Seerah
sacred_texts.description: Biographical accounts of the life of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, providing context and guidance.

cultural_contributions: Algebra — the word 'algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr' (Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, 9th century)
Preservation and advancement of Greek philosophy through the Islamic Golden Age
Hospitals and medical schools — Ibn Sina's 'Canon of Medicine' was used in Europe for centuries
Astronomy — Arabic names of many stars; development of the astrolabe
Architecture — domes, minarets, geometric art; Alhambra, Blue Mosque, Hagia Sophia conversions
Calligraphy as a major art form
Coffee — originated in Yemen and spread to the world through the Ottoman Empire

respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_judaism: Islam, Judaism, and Christianity are the three Abrahamic faiths — all trace their spiritual lineage to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). Jews and Muslims both follow detailed religious law (Halakha and Sharia respectively), avoid pork, and share reverence for many of the same prophets.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_christianity: Muslims believe in Jesus (Isa) as a revered prophet and the Messiah. Both faiths emphasise prayer, charity, fasting, and caring for the poor. The Golden Rule — treat others as you wish to be treated — appears in both traditions.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_hinduism: Both traditions emphasise daily prayer and worship, the importance of family, charitable giving, and the value of fasting. Some Sufi practices share similarities with Hindu devotional traditions.
respectful_comparisons.note: These comparisons are meant to highlight shared human values. Each religion has its own distinct theology, practices, and history.

christianity.name: Christianity
christianity.summary: Christianity is a monotheistic faith based on the life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God who died for humanity's sins and rose from the dead. The faith has three main branches: Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant.

history.event: Birth of Jesus of Nazareth in Bethlehem
Crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus; founding of the early Church
Missionary journeys of Paul; spread of Christianity across the Roman Empire
Edict of Milan — Emperor Constantine legalises Christianity in the Roman Empire
Christianity becomes the official religion of the Roman Empire
Great Schism — split between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches
Martin Luther's 95 Theses — beginning of the Protestant Reformation
Christian missionary activity globally; growth of Christianity in Africa, Asia, and Latin America

core_tenets: The Trinity — God as Father, Son (Jesus Christ), and Holy Spirit
Jesus as saviour — through his death and resurrection, sins are forgiven
The Bible as the inspired word of God
Prayer and personal relationship with God
Baptism and other sacraments (varies by denomination)

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.description: Celebration of the birth of Jesus. Observed with church services, gift-giving, family gatherings, and seasonal traditions.

festivals.name: Easter
festivals.timing: First Sunday after the first full moon after 21 March
festivals.description: The most important Christian festival — celebrating the resurrection of Jesus after his crucifixion. Preceded by Lent (40 days of fasting and reflection) and Holy Week.

festivals.name: Good Friday
festivals.description: Commemorates the crucifixion of Jesus. Observed with fasting, prayer, and sombre services.

festivals.name: Pentecost
festivals.description: Celebrates the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles. Considered the birthday of the Christian Church.

festivals.name: Advent
festivals.description: Period of preparation and anticipation before Christmas, observed with prayer, reflection, and Advent calendars.

sacred_texts.name: The Bible
sacred_texts.description: The central scripture of Christianity, consisting of the Old Testament (shared with Judaism) and the New Testament (accounts of Jesus's life, early church letters, and Revelation). Different denominations use slightly different canons.

sacred_texts.name: The Gospels
sacred_texts.description: Four accounts of Jesus's life and teachings: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The core of the New Testament.

cultural_contributions: Preservation of classical learning during the Medieval period through monasteries
Foundation of universities — Oxford, Cambridge, Bologna, and many others were founded by the Church
Gothic cathedral architecture — Notre Dame, Chartres, Canterbury
The works of Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, and Raphael inspired by Christian themes
Music — Bach, Handel's Messiah, Gregorian chant
Hospital and charity systems — inspired by the Christian call to care for the sick and poor
The Gregorian calendar used worldwide

respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_judaism: Christianity grew from Jewish roots — Jesus was Jewish, as were his disciples. Christians revere the Hebrew scriptures as the Old Testament. Both traditions emphasise the Ten Commandments, love of God, care for the poor, and justice.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_islam: Both are Abrahamic monotheistic faiths. Muslims hold Jesus in deep respect as a prophet. Both emphasise prayer, charity, fasting, and compassion for others. The Golden Rule appears in both.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_buddhism: Both traditions emphasise compassion, non-violence, and helping those who suffer. Christian monastic traditions (like those of St Francis of Assisi) share similarities with Buddhist approaches to simplicity and community.
respectful_comparisons.note: These comparisons highlight shared values. Each religion has distinct theology and history.

hinduism.name: Hinduism
hinduism.founded: c. 1500 BCE or earlier (one of the world's oldest religions)
hinduism.summary: Hinduism is one of the world's oldest religious traditions, originating on the Indian subcontinent. Unlike religions with a single founder, Hinduism is a rich, diverse family of beliefs and practices. Central concepts include Dharma (righteous duty), Karma (actions and their consequences), Moksha (liberation from the cycle of rebirth), and Samsara (the cycle of death and rebirth).

history.event: Vedic period — composition of the Rigveda; earliest Hindu scriptures
Upanishadic period — philosophical texts exploring the nature of reality, self, and Brahman
Composition of the Mahabharata (including the Bhagavad Gita) and Ramayana
Gupta period — classical age of Hindu art, architecture, and philosophy
Adi Shankaracharya revitalises Hindu philosophy; temple-building era
Bhakti movement — devotional saints like Kabir and Mirabai emphasise personal love of God over ritual
Hindu Renaissance — Ramakrishna, Vivekananda, Mahatma Gandhi bring Hindu philosophy to global attention

core_concepts: Dharma — moral duty and righteous living
Karma — law of cause and effect across lifetimes
Samsara — cycle of birth, death, and rebirth

festivals.name: Diwali
festivals.description: Festival of Lights — celebrating the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance. Homes are decorated with oil lamps, fireworks are lit, sweets are shared, and Lakshmi (goddess of prosperity) is worshipped.

festivals.name: Holi
festivals.description: Festival of Colours — celebrating the arrival of spring and the victory of good over evil (the story of Prahlada and Holika). People throw coloured powder and water at each other in joyful celebration.

festivals.name: Navratri & Dussehra
festivals.description: Nine nights of worship of the goddess Durga, followed by Dussehra — celebrating the victory of Rama over Ravana (good over evil).

festivals.name: Janmashtami
festivals.description: Celebration of the birth of Lord Krishna — midnight prayers, fasting, singing, and re-enactments of Krishna's life.

festivals.name: Maha Shivaratri
festivals.description: The Great Night of Shiva — fasting, all-night prayers, and devotional singing in honour of Lord Shiva.

sacred_texts.name: The Vedas
sacred_texts.description: The oldest Hindu scriptures, composed in Sanskrit: Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda. Considered shruti ('that which is heard') — divinely revealed knowledge.

sacred_texts.name: The Upanishads
sacred_texts.description: Philosophical texts exploring the nature of Brahman, Atman, and reality. The foundation of Hindu philosophical schools (Vedanta).

sacred_texts.name: The Bhagavad Gita
sacred_texts.description: A 700-verse dialogue between Prince Arjuna and Lord Krishna, part of the Mahabharata. One of the most widely read spiritual texts in the world, covering duty, devotion, and liberation.

sacred_texts.name: The Ramayana
sacred_texts.description: Epic poem telling the story of Rama's quest to rescue his wife Sita. A moral guide for righteous conduct.

sacred_texts.name: The Mahabharata
sacred_texts.description: One of the longest epics in world literature, containing the Bhagavad Gita and exploring themes of duty, war, and justice.

cultural_contributions: Yoga — now practised worldwide as physical and mental wellness
Ayurveda — traditional medicine system influencing global wellness
Sanskrit — one of the world's oldest languages; root of many Indo-European languages
Mathematics — the concept of zero, decimal notation, and early algebra (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta)
Music — classical Indian music traditions (Carnatic, Hindustani)
Architecture — temple art, Angkor Wat (Cambodia), Prambanan (Indonesia)
Philosophy — Vedanta philosophy influenced Western philosophers including Schopenhauer and Emerson

respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_buddhism: Buddhism arose from the Hindu tradition — the Buddha was a Hindu prince. Both share concepts of karma, samsara, dharma, and the goal of liberation from suffering. Both emphasise meditation, non-violence (ahimsa), and compassion.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_islam: Both traditions emphasise daily prayer and worship, fasting, charity, the importance of family, and pilgrimage. Sufi mystical traditions within Islam share similarities with Hindu devotional (Bhakti) practices.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_christianity: Both traditions have rich traditions of devotional love of God, charitable service, and festivals celebrating the victory of good over evil. Mahatma Gandhi was deeply influenced by the Sermon on the Mount.
respectful_comparisons.note: Hinduism is highly diverse — practices and beliefs vary enormously. These comparisons focus on broad shared values.

buddhism.name: Buddhism
buddhism.summary: Buddhism is a spiritual tradition founded on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha ('the Awakened One'). Buddhism teaches that suffering arises from craving and ignorance, and that liberation (Nirvana) is achieved through wisdom, ethical conduct, and meditation. Buddhism has two major traditions: Theravada (Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia) and Mahayana (East Asia, including Tibetan Buddhism).

history.event: Birth of Siddhartha Gautama (the future Buddha) in Lumbini (modern Nepal)
Siddhartha attains enlightenment under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya
First sermon at Deer Park, Sarnath — Buddha teaches the Four Noble Truths
Parinirvana (death) of the Buddha; first Buddhist council to preserve his teachings
Emperor Ashoka converts to Buddhism and spreads it across India and beyond
Mahayana Buddhism emerges; Buddhism spreads to China, Korea, Japan, and Southeast Asia
Vajrayana (Tibetan) Buddhism develops; Buddhism spreads to Tibet
Buddhist revival and spread to the West; Zen and Tibetan traditions become globally known

four_noble_truths: Dukkha: Life involves suffering and dissatisfaction
Samudaya: Suffering arises from craving and ignorance
Nirodha: Suffering can end — through the cessation of craving
Magga: The Eightfold Path is the way to end suffering

festivals.name: Vesak (Buddha Day)
festivals.description: The most important Buddhist festival — celebrating the birth, enlightenment, and death of the Buddha. Observed with meditation, temple visits, releasing lanterns, and charitable acts.

festivals.name: Losar
festivals.description: Tibetan Buddhist New Year — celebrated with prayers, rituals, and dances to welcome the new year and drive away evil.

festivals.name: Vassa (Rains Retreat)
festivals.description: A period of retreat and intensive practice for monks and nuns, traditionally when the Buddha limited travel during the rainy season.

festivals.name: Kathina
festivals.description: Celebration marking the end of the retreat — laypeople offer robes and supplies to monks in an act of generosity.

sacred_texts.name: Tipitaka (Pali Canon)
sacred_texts.description: The earliest Buddhist scriptures, preserved in the Pali language. Contains the Vinaya (monastic rules), Sutta Pitaka (discourses of the Buddha), and Abhidhamma (philosophical analysis).

sacred_texts.name: Dhammapada
sacred_texts.description: A beloved collection of 423 verses attributed to the Buddha, covering the nature of the mind and the path to liberation.

sacred_texts.name: Heart Sutra
sacred_texts.description: A key Mahayana text exploring the concept of emptiness (sunyata). Widely chanted in East Asian Buddhist traditions.

cultural_contributions: Mindfulness meditation — now widely practised in secular mental health settings worldwide
Buddhist art and architecture — stupas, pagodas, Buddha statues (Borobudur, Angkor Wat elements)
Influence on East Asian cultures — Japanese Zen, Chinese Chan, Korean Son
Non-violence as political philosophy — Mahatma Gandhi was influenced by Buddhist principles; the Dalai Lama's peace advocacy
Monastic education systems — early universities in Nalanda, India, attracted scholars from across Asia
Environmental philosophy — emphasis on compassion for all living beings has influenced environmental ethics

respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_hinduism: Buddhism shares with Hinduism the concepts of karma, samsara, and dharma. Both emphasise meditation, non-violence (ahimsa), and the search for liberation. The Buddha himself came from the Hindu tradition.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_christianity: Both emphasise compassion, service to the poor and suffering, and the transformation of the inner self. Christian monastic traditions share similarities with Buddhist monastery practices.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_islam: Both emphasise self-discipline, meditation/prayer, charitable giving, and care for others. Sufi Islamic mysticism shares some similarities with Buddhist contemplative practices.
respectful_comparisons.note: Buddhism is diverse — Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana traditions vary considerably.

judaism.name: Judaism
judaism.summary: Judaism is the world's oldest Abrahamic monotheistic religion, the faith from which Christianity and Islam both trace roots. Jews believe in one God who made a covenant with the Jewish people. Judaism emphasises ethical conduct, study of scripture, and communal observance. Major movements include Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, and Liberal Judaism.

history.event: Abraham — father of the Jewish people — receives the covenant with God
Exodus from Egypt; Moses receives the Torah at Mount Sinai
Kingdom of Israel under King David; Jerusalem established as capital
Solomon's Temple built in Jerusalem — the First Temple
Babylonian Exile — Temple destroyed; Jewish people exiled to Babylon
Second Temple built; Jews return to the Land of Israel
Roman destruction of the Second Temple; beginning of the Jewish Diaspora
Establishment of the State of Israel

core_tenets: Monotheism — belief in one God, indivisible
The Covenant — God's special relationship with the Jewish people
Torah as divine law and guide for life
The importance of ethical conduct (Tikkun Olam — repairing the world)
The coming of the Messiah (a future leader who will bring world peace)
Life in this world is valued; focus on living righteously now
beliefs.613_commandments: The Torah contains 613 mitzvot (commandments) covering every aspect of life — prayer, food, business ethics, family relations. Different movements interpret and apply these differently.

festivals.name: Rosh Hashanah
festivals.description: Jewish New Year — a day of prayer, reflection, and hearing the shofar (ram's horn). Begins 10 days of repentance.

festivals.name: Yom Kippur
festivals.description: Day of Atonement — the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. A 25-hour fast with prayer and reflection on the past year's actions and seeking forgiveness.

festivals.name: Passover (Pesach)
festivals.description: Celebrates the Exodus from slavery in Egypt. A Seder meal retells the story; special dietary laws (no leavened bread — matzah is eaten).

festivals.name: Hanukkah
festivals.description: Festival of Lights — eight-night celebration commemorating the rededication of the Temple. A menorah (hanukkiah) is lit each night; gifts and games (dreidel) are traditional.

festivals.name: Shabbat
festivals.timing: Weekly — Friday sundown to Saturday night
festivals.description: The day of rest — in memory of God's rest on the seventh day. Observed with candle lighting, family meals, prayer, and rest from work.

sacred_texts.name: The Torah
sacred_texts.description: The five books of Moses (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy). The central sacred text of Judaism.

sacred_texts.name: The Tanakh
sacred_texts.description: The complete Hebrew Bible — Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings). What Christians call the Old Testament.

sacred_texts.name: The Talmud
sacred_texts.description: A vast collection of rabbinic discussion, legal reasoning, and commentary on the Torah. The foundation of Jewish law (Halacha) and ethics.

cultural_contributions: Monotheism — the idea of one universal God influenced both Christianity and Islam
The Ten Commandments — foundational to Western legal and moral traditions
Jewish Nobel laureates — despite being 0.2% of the world's population, Jewish people have won approximately 22% of Nobel Prizes
Sigmund Freud (psychoanalysis), Albert Einstein (physics), Franz Kafka (literature), Marc Chagall (art)
Tzedakah (charity) — Jewish tradition of giving has inspired many philanthropic practices
The Sabbath concept — weekly rest influenced labour laws worldwide

respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_christianity: Christianity grew directly from Judaism — Jesus, his disciples, and the early church were all Jewish. Christians share the Hebrew scriptures (Old Testament) and revere many of the same prophets. Both traditions emphasise love of God and neighbour.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_islam: Judaism and Islam are both Abrahamic, strictly monotheistic, follow detailed religious law (Halacha / Sharia), and consider Abraham a forefather. Both share dietary laws (kosher / halal), reject images of God, and stress social justice.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_buddhism: Both traditions value ethical conduct, study, and wisdom. Tikkun Olam (repairing the world) in Judaism parallels the Bodhisattva ideal of compassionate service in Mahayana Buddhism.
respectful_comparisons.note: Judaism is diverse — Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, and other movements have varying practices and interpretations.

sikhism.name: Sikhism
sikhism.summary: Sikhism is a monotheistic faith founded by Guru Nanak Dev Ji in the 15th century in the Punjab region. Sikhs believe in one God (Waheguru — the Wonderful Lord), equality of all people regardless of caste, gender, or religion, and service to humanity (Seva). The faith developed through ten human Gurus and continues through the eternal Guru — the Guru Granth Sahib (the holy scripture).

history.event: Birth of Guru Nanak Dev Ji — founder of Sikhism — in Nankana Sahib (modern Pakistan)
Guru Nanak's divine experience at the river — begins his spiritual mission; 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim'
Nine more human Gurus guide the Sikh community and develop its institutions
Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiles the Adi Granth (original scripture) and installs it in the Golden Temple
Guru Gobind Singh Ji establishes the Khalsa — the community of initiated Sikhs — and introduces the Five Ks
Guru Gobind Singh Ji declares the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal, living Guru
Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh at its height
Partition of India — Punjab divided; mass migration of Sikhs

core_tenets: Waheguru — belief in one eternal, formless God
Equality of all people — no caste, gender, or religious discrimination
Three pillars: Naam Japna (meditating on God), Kirat Karna (earning honestly), Vand Chhakna (sharing with others)
The ten human Gurus as spiritual teachers
Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal, living Guru
five_ks: Kesh — uncut hair (covered by a turban for men)
Kara — steel bracelet (reminder of God and the Guru)
Kirpan — ceremonial steel sword (courage and defence of the weak)

festivals.name: Gurpurabs
festivals.description: Celebrations of the birthdays and martyrdoms of the Gurus. The most important are the birthdays of Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Guru Gobind Singh Ji. Observed with prayers, kirtan (devotional music), and langar (community meals).

festivals.name: Vaisakhi (Baisakhi)
festivals.description: Sikh New Year and harvest festival — also marks the founding of the Khalsa in 1699 by Guru Gobind Singh Ji. Celebrated with prayers, processions, and kirtan.

festivals.name: Hola Mohalla
festivals.description: Established by Guru Gobind Singh Ji as a day of martial arts demonstrations, poetry, and music — a demonstration of Sikh courage and community.

festivals.name: Diwali (Bandhi Chhor Divas)
festivals.description: Sikhs celebrate Diwali as Bandhi Chhor Divas — the day Guru Hargobind Ji was released from imprisonment and freed 52 other prisoners too. The Golden Temple is illuminated.

sacred_texts.name: Guru Granth Sahib
sacred_texts.description: The eternal, living Guru of the Sikhs — the holy scripture containing the hymns of the Sikh Gurus and saints of other faiths. Written in Gurmukhi script. Treated with the same reverence as a living Guru.

sacred_texts.name: Nitnem
sacred_texts.description: Daily prayers recited by observant Sikhs, drawn from the Guru Granth Sahib. Includes the morning Japji Sahib (composed by Guru Nanak).

cultural_contributions: The concept of the Langar (free community kitchen) — the Golden Temple in Amritsar serves 100,000 free meals per day, open to all regardless of religion, caste, or background
Martial arts traditions — Gatka (Sikh martial art)
Architecture — the Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) in Amritsar is one of the world's most visited sites
Social reform — Sikhism actively opposed the caste system and gender inequality centuries before modern social movements
Music — Kirtan (devotional music) tradition; tabla and harmonium in Sikh worship
Military contribution — Sikh soldiers served with distinction in both World Wars

respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_islam: Both are strictly monotheistic, emphasise equality regardless of birth or status, value prayer and charity, and are wary of idol worship. Guru Nanak was deeply influenced by both Hindu and Muslim traditions and sought common ground between them.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_hinduism: Sikhism arose in the Hindu cultural context of Punjab. The Guru Granth Sahib includes writings from Hindu and Sufi saints. Both traditions value devotion (bhakti), karma, and dharma.
respectful_comparisons.common_ground_with_christianity: Both emphasise service to others, equality before God, and a personal relationship with the divine. The Golden Rule — treat others as you wish to be treated — is central to both.
respectful_comparisons.note: Sikhism is a distinct, independent religion, not a blend of Hinduism and Islam.
